# xgbexcel

> xgbexcel converts a trained XGBoost model into an Excel formula, so it can be scored
> in a spreadsheet without Python or add-ins.

## Key Facts

- Converts XGBoost regressors and classifiers into nested Excel IF formulas
- Works with XGBoost 1.7 through 3.x
- Handles multiclass (softmax), binary (sigmoid), multi-output regression, vector
  leaves, forest mode, dart and early stopping
- Reproduces XGBoost's float32 branch decisions from a float64 Excel comparison
- Raises UnsupportedModelError rather than emitting a formula that is quietly wrong
- Installable via pip: `pip install xgbexcel`
- MIT licensed, Python 3.9+

## When to Use xgbexcel

- You need to score a small XGBoost model in Excel and cannot install a runtime
- You want to hand a model to someone who works in spreadsheets
- You want a readable formula representation of a small tree ensemble

## When Not to Use It

- Excel caps formulas at 8192 characters. A default 100-tree, depth-6 model produces
  roughly 150,000 characters, so only small models fit in a single cell.
- Blank cells are not missing values; Excel reads a blank as 0.
- If you can install a runtime, ONNX (via onnxmltools) is a better deployment path.

## Links

- Repository: https://github.com/KalinNonchev/xgbexcel
- PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/xgbexcel/

## Installation

```
pip install xgbexcel
```

## Quick Start

```python
from xgbexcel import XGBtoExcel
from xgboost import XGBRegressor

model = XGBRegressor(n_estimators=3, max_depth=2).fit(X_train, y_train)

formula = XGBtoExcel(model, feature_names=["Age", "Income"])
print(formula.expression)

formula.save_expr("model_formula.txt")
```

Multi-output models expose one formula per output through `formula.expressions`.
